status: Primary wetting evidence and explicit electrical-contact data gap; no simulation calibration

sources.title: Wettability of Pure Metals with Liquid Sodium and Liquid Tin
sources.evidence: Full primary HTML and Figure4 inspected. Pure liquid Sn at530K in argon: oxygen<3ppm and moisture2.6ppm. Polished substrates; SUS304 is a reference. Figure4b suggests about30deg onCu and130deg onSUS304; these are approximate graph readings, not fitted model inputs.
sources.limits: PureSn, notSn99.3Cu0.7 or60/40. SUS304, not316. Does not measure specific electrical contact resistivity. Surface history and drop scale differ from this head.

sources.title: Wettability of Liquid Tin on Solid Copper
sources.evidence: Primary abstract inspected. At340C, oxidizedCu with roughly60nmCu2O gives about half the tin spreading area of the unoxidized comparison.
sources.limits: Differenttemperature and surface preparation. Spreading area is not an electrical-contact-resistivity measurement.

sources.title: Non-wetting to Wetting Transition Temperatures of Liquid Tin on Surfaces of Different Steel Samples Corresponding to their Spontaneous Deoxidation
sources.evidence: Primary paper inspected. Initially oxidized steels in high vacuum remain nonwetting near tin melting; wetting transitions occur at substantially higher temperatures.
sources.limits: Steels tested areC45,S103,CK60,EN1.4034, not our316. These high-temperature transition data are not250C wetting-angle or electrical-contact calibration.

what_was_not_found: No defensible measured specific electrical contact resistivity for this SnCu/solder/stainless/Cu geometry and preparation at operating temperature. The1e-9ohmm2 simulation remains an explicitly assumed sensitivity, not a literature-derived nominal value.
design_inferences: Material-dependent wetting deserves attention: wetted copper electrodes could aid current transfer while relatively nonwetting stainless end walls could aid confinement. This is a testable design hypothesis, not established head performance.

A uniform neutral-wall fluid treatment and a uniform electrical-interface parameter do not capture these different surface states. Contact angle does not uniquely determine electrical contact resistivity.
Better wetting can also encourage unwanted film spreading. Integral stainless end walls still need a real hot seal against the copper plates; material choice alone does not close a seam.
targeted_measurement_outline: Measure sessile-drop advancing/receding behavior on actual machined/preparedCu and316 coupons with each solder and the intended atmosphere/temperature; record preparation and timehistory.

Characterize electrical transfer in a known insulating bath fixture that prevents a steel-wall bypass. Use separate current/sense connections and reversed low-current readings to distinguish resistance from thermoelectric offsets.
Use geometry/area variation and bulk-current modeling to separate interface effects from liquid spreading resistance. Total head resistance alone can hide poor liquid transfer behind a metal shunt.

Only after low-current characterization, compare pulse-shapedV/I/contact behavior under the intended drive. Do not assume ohmic contact or transfer a fitted coefficient across different surface preparations.
scope: These are proposed characterization steps, not tests performed or instructions to purchase hardware. No model input, native result or frozen simulator baseline changed.
